# The Heat Is Uneven: How Cities Can Make Summer More Bearable

On a hot August afternoon, the temperature difference between two neighborhoods in the same city can exceed ten degrees Fahrenheit. This is not a matter of weather, which does not vary across a few blocks, but of design. Cities are built environments, and the way we build them determines who swelters and who finds relief. As climate change lengthens and intensifies heat waves, urban heat has become a public health crisis—heat kills more Americans annually than hurricanes, floods, and tornadoes combined. The good news is that cities have proven tools to fight back. The challenge is that these tools require money, space, and political will, and they involve genuine tradeoffs that residents must weigh.

## Trees: The Oldest Air Conditioner

The single most effective intervention against urban heat is also the most ancient: shade. Trees cool cities in two ways. Their canopies block solar radiation before it hits pavement, and their leaves release water vapor through transpiration, a natural evaporative cooling process. A mature street tree can lower the surface temperature beneath it by twenty to forty degrees compared to exposed asphalt. Neighborhoods with dense tree cover can be several degrees cooler than treeless areas just a mile away.
